source_text: Καὶ τὸν μὲν οὐδεὶς ἂν ἀποκτεῖναι τολμήσειεν, εἰς τὸν Θεὸν ἀσεβεῖν ἡγούμενος, εἰ τὸν τοιοῦτον ἀνέλοι· τῷ δὲ πολλοὶ σφαγεῖς ἐφεστήκασιν ἐρασταὶ τυραννίδος. Διόπερ ὁ μὲν φρουρεῖται στρατιώταις, ὁ δὲ πόλεις τειχίζει ταῖς εὐχαῖς, οὐδένα δεδοικώς· ὁ δὲ βασιλεὺς ἀεὶ φόβῳ συζῇ καὶ προσδοκίᾳ σφαγῆς· ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἐπικίνδυνον ἔχει πλεονεξίαν, ὁ δὲ ἀσφαλῆ σωτηρίαν. Περὶ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἐν τῷ παρόντι βίῳ πραγμάτων ἱκανῶς εἰρῆσθαί μοι δοκεῖ. Εἰ δὲ καὶ τὸν ἀγῶνα τὸν μέλλοντα βουληθείημεν ἐξετάζειν, τὸν μὲν ὀψόμεθα λαμπρὸν καὶ περίβλεπτον ἁρπαζόμενον ἐν νεφέλαις εἰς ἀπάντησιν τοῦ Κυρίου εἰς ἀέρα, κατὰ τὸν ἡγεμόνα καὶ παιδευτὴν τοῦ σωτηρίου τούτου βίου καὶ πάσης ἀρετῆς· ὁ δὲ βασιλεὺς, ἐὰν μὲν δικαίως φανείη καὶ φιλανθρώπως διοικήσας τὴν ἀρχὴν πολὺ δὲ τοῦτο σπάνιον, ἐλάττονος ἔσται σωτηρίας τε καὶ τιμῆς· οὐ γὰρ ἴσον, οὐκ ἴσον βασιλεύς τε χρηστὸς καὶ μοναχὸς ἄκρως τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ λατρείᾳ συζῶν. Εἰ δὲ φανείη πονηρὸς καὶ σκαιὸς, πολλῶν κακῶν ἐμπεπληκὼς τὴν γῆν, τίς ἂν εἰπεῖν δυνηθείη τὰς συμφορὰς αἷς ὀφθήσεται συνεχόμενος, πυρὶ καιόμενος, μαστιγούμενος, στρεβλούμενος, τοιαῦτα πάσχων ἅπερ οὔτε λόγῳ ῥητὰ, οὐδὲ ἔργῳ φορητά; Ταῦτα πάντα δεῖ λογιζομένους καὶ μανθάνοντας, μὴ τοὺς πλουτοῦντας θαυμάζειν· ὁ γὰρ τούτων δεσπότης πεφηνὼς, οὐδὲ κατὰ μικρὸν ἐγγὺς ἐλθεῖν δύναται τῆς τοῦ μοναχοῦ ἀρετῆς. Ὅταν οὖν ἴδῃς πλούσιον ἐσθῆτι κεκοσμημένον, χρυσῷ καλλωπιζόμενον, ἐπ' ὀχημάτων φερόμενον, ἐξόδους ἐξιόντα λαμπρὰς, μὴ μακαρίσῃς τὸν ἄνθρωπον· πρόσκαιρος γὰρ ὁ πλοῦτος, καὶ τὸ δοκοῦν εἶναι καλὸν τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ συνδιαφθείρεται· μοναχὸν δὲ ἰδὼν βαδίζοντα μόνον, ταπεινὸν καὶ πρᾶον καὶ ἡσύχιον καὶ ἥμερον, ζήλωσον τὸν ἄνδρα, φάνηθι μιμητὴς τῆς ἐκείνου φιλοσοφίας, εὖξαι γενέσθαι τῷ δικαίῳ παραπλήσιος· Αἰτεῖτε γὰρ, φησὶ, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν. Ταῦτα γὰρ ὡς ἀληθῶς καλὰ καὶ σωτήρια καὶ μόνιμα, διὰ τὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ φιλανθρωπίαν καὶ πρόνοιαν· ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.
thought_title: The monk's security and the king's danger, and the final exhortation
orientation: Chrysostom is concluding his comparison of the king and the monk, showing that the monk is safe from murder while the king lives in fear, then turning to the future judgment and a final exhortation to imitate the monk rather than admire the rich.
pass_a_gloss: And the former no one would dare to kill, considering it impiety toward God, if he should slay such a man; but against the latter many slayers stand ready, lovers of tyranny. Therefore the former is guarded by soldiers, but the latter walls cities with his prayers, fearing no one; but the king always lives with fear and expectation of slaughter; for the former has dangerous greed, but the latter secure salvation. Concerning the matters in the present life, then, it seems to me enough has been said. But if we should wish to examine also the coming contest, we shall see the former bright and conspicuous being snatched up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air, like the leader and teacher of this saving way of life and of all virtue; but the king, if he should appear having administered his rule justly and with love for humanity—but this is very rare—will be of lesser salvation and honor; for it is not equal, not equal, a good king and a monk living at the peak in the service of God. But if he should appear wicked and harsh, having filled the earth with many evils, who could tell the disasters by which he will be seen to be held fast, burning with fire, being scourged, being tortured, suffering such things as are neither speakable in word nor bearable in deed? Considering and learning all these things, we must not admire the rich; for the one who has appeared as master of these things cannot come even a little near to the virtue of the monk. Whenever, then, you see a rich man adorned with clothing, beautified with gold, carried on chariots, making splendid public appearances, do not call the man blessed; for wealth is temporary, and what seems to be beautiful is destroyed together with this life; but seeing a monk walking alone, humble and gentle and quiet and mild, be zealous for the man, become an imitator of his way of life, pray to become like the righteous man; For ask, it says, and it will be given to you. For these things are truly beautiful and saving and lasting, through the love for humanity and providence of Christ; to whom be the glory and the might forever and ever. Amen.

choices.term: ὁ μὲν φρουρεῖται στρατιώταις, ὁ δὲ πόλεις τειχίζει ταῖς εὐχαῖς
choices.english: the former is guarded by soldiers, but the latter walls cities with his prayers
choices.why: The μὲν...δὲ contrast refers back to the monk (former) and king (latter) from the previous sentence; the monk is guarded by soldiers (angels or spiritual protection), while the king fortifies cities with prayers (i.e., relies on the prayers of monks).
rejected: the king is guarded by soldiers, while the monk walls cities with his prayers

choices.term: ὁ μὲν γὰρ ἐπικίνδυνον ἔχει πλεονεξίαν, ὁ δὲ ἀσφαλῆ σωτηρίαν
choices.english: for the former has dangerous greed, but the latter secure salvation
choices.why: The former is the king (whose greed for power is dangerous), the latter the monk (whose salvation is secure); πλεονεξίαν is greed/covetousness, not 'excess of power.'
rejected: the king's dangerous excess of power brings danger

choices.term: κατὰ τὸν ἡγεμόνα καὶ παιδευτὴν τοῦ σωτηρίου τούτου βίου καὶ πάσης ἀρετῆς
choices.english: like the leader and teacher of this saving way of life and of all virtue
choices.why: κατὰ with accusative here means 'in the manner of' or 'like,' indicating the monk is snatched up in the same way as the leader and teacher (Paul, the apostle).
rejected: according to the leader and teacher of this saving way of life and of all virtue

choices.why: Per glossary, φιλοσοφία is rendered 'way of life' for the monastic life.
Per glossary, φιλανθρωπία is rendered 'love for humanity' for Christ's love.

choices.term: ἐν νεφέλαις εἰς ἀπάντησιν τοῦ Κυρίου εἰς ἀέρα
choices.english: in clouds to meet the Lord in the air
choices.why: Echoes 1 Thessalonians 4:17 language; rendered literally to preserve the eschatological imagery.
rejected: on clouds to the meeting of the Lord in the air

pass_b_english: No one would dare to kill the monk, because he would consider it an act of impiety against God to destroy such a man. But many slayers stand over the king, lovers of tyranny. So the king is guarded by soldiers, while the monk walls cities with his prayers, fearing no one. The king, however, always lives with fear and the expectation of slaughter. For the king has dangerous greed, but the monk has secure salvation. Now I think enough has been said about the affairs of this present life. But if we should wish to examine the contest that is to come, we will see the monk shining and admired, snatched up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:17), like the leader and teacher of this saving way of life and of all virtue. The king, if he appears to have ruled his power justly and with love for humanity—though this is very rare—will receive lesser salvation and honor. For it is not equal, not equal: a good king and a monk living at the height of service to God. But if the king appears wicked and perverse, having filled the earth with many evils, who could describe the disasters that will be seen pressing upon him—burned with fire, scourged, tortured, suffering things that cannot be spoken in words or endured in deed? Considering and learning all these things, we must not admire the rich. For the one who has become master of these things cannot come even a little close to the virtue of the monk. So when you see a rich man adorned with clothing, beautified with gold, carried on chariots, making splendid public appearances, do not call that man blessed. For wealth is temporary, and what seems beautiful in this life is destroyed along with it. But when you see a monk walking alone, humble and gentle and quiet and mild, emulate that man. Show yourself an imitator of his way of life. Pray to become like that righteous man. For it says, “Ask, and it will be given to you” (Matthew 7:7). These things are truly good and saving and lasting, through the love for humanity and providence of Christ, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
